Open models on your own computer

Source: vignettes/open-models.Rmd
open-models.Rmd
library(decisions)

Overview

Laya is an open decision model from Convai Innovations (Apache 2.0 license). It runs on a CPU. You start a server on your computer, and the decisions package talks to it. The texts stay on your computer. No key is needed, and a call has no cost.

Laya speaks the SystemOne format, as Jev does. So only the decider changes. The questions and the call of decide() stay the same.

Laya reads text only. It does not read images.

The section Venn shows a second open model, Venn, and a calibration step for its probabilities.

The results below come from a live run on a CPU. The package saved them in the package folder extdata, so this vignette builds without Laya and without a network. The code that made them is in vignette_results.R in the folder data-raw of the GitHub repository.

Install

Laya needs Python. The commands below make an environment and install the server. They do not run when this vignette builds.

conda create -y -n laya python=3.11
conda activate laya
pip install "laya[serve]"

Start

Set the device and the port, then start the server. The first start downloads three checkpoints from Hugging Face (english, multilingual and typed-decisions) and loads them. On our computer, the start took about one minute.

LAYA_DEVICE=cpu LAYA_PORT=8000 laya-serve

In PowerShell, set the variables first:

$env:LAYA_DEVICE = "cpu"
$env:LAYA_PORT = "8000"
laya-serve

The server is ready when the health check answers.

curl http://localhost:8000/health

To stop the server, press Ctrl+C in its window.

Decider

decider_systemone() takes the URL of the server and the name of a checkpoint. Only the URL and the model differ from the Jev decider of the other vignettes. The decider sends no key, because it has no credentials. input = "text" makes decide() stop if you give it an image.

laya <- decider_systemone("http://localhost:8000", "english", input = "text")
laya
#> <decider> The server at http://localhost:8000
#> * Model: english
#> * URL: http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone
#> * Request format: systemone
#> * Input: text

Data and questions

This vignette stands alone, so it defines the tickets and the questions again. They are the same as in the vignette “Getting started with text”. We wrote the tickets for these vignettes.

tickets <- tibble::tibble(
  ticket = 1:10,
  text = c(
    "I was charged twice for order 4471. Please refund the extra charge today.",
    "My parcel has not arrived. The tracking page has said 'in transit' for two weeks.",
    "The app crashes each time I open the settings page. I cannot log in, and I have a meeting in ten minutes.",
    "Thank you for the quick delivery. The product works well.",
    "I want my money back. The blender broke after one day.",
    "How do I change the email address on my account?",
    "The invoice shows the wrong company name. Please send a new one when you can.",
    "The package arrived with a broken seal. Please send a replacement. There is no hurry.",
    "Your website shows an error when I pay by card. I must order before the sale ends tonight.",
    "Can you tell me which sizes the jacket comes in?"
  )
)

refund <- question_noul("Does the customer ask for a refund?")

topic <- question_choice(
  "Which team should answer this ticket?",
  c(
    billing = "Charges, invoices and refunds.",
    shipping = "Parcels and delivery.",
    technical = "Errors, and how to use the product."
  )
)

urgency <- question_score(
  "How urgent is this ticket?",
  c(
    low = "The customer can wait several days.",
    medium = "The customer needs an answer today.",
    high = "The customer needs an answer now."
  )
)

Decisions

One call of decide() asks the three questions about the ten tickets. We set max_active = 1, so the server gets one request at a time. Then .seconds is the time that the CPU needs for one request. With more active requests, the requests wait for each other on a CPU.

answers <- decide(
  laya,
  list(refund = refund, topic = topic, urgency = urgency),
  text = tickets$text,
  max_active = 1
)

decide() prints one message, because Laya does not report a cost. The message says that the server at http://localhost:8000 reports no cost, that .cost is NA, and that .input_tokens has the input tokens. The model that the server reports is laya-rl-agent, whatever the checkpoint.

dplyr::bind_cols(
  tickets["ticket"],
  answers[c("refund_.pred_class", "topic_.pred_class", "urgency_.pred_class", ".seconds")]
)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    ticket refund_.pred_class topic_.pred_class urgency_.pred_class .seconds
#>     <int> <fct>              <fct>             <fct>                  <dbl>
#>  1      1 true               billing           medium                 0.461
#>  2      2 false              shipping          medium                 0.713
#>  3      3 false              technical         medium                 0.501
#>  4      4 false              shipping          medium                 0.478
#>  5      5 true               technical         medium                 0.448
#>  6      6 false              technical         medium                 0.418
#>  7      7 true               billing           medium                 0.465
#>  8      8 true               shipping          low                    0.485
#>  9      9 false              billing           medium                 0.477
#> 10     10 false              shipping          medium                 0.463

Time 

dplyr::summarise(
  answers,
  rows = dplyr::n(),
  errors = sum(!is.na(.error)),
  input_tokens = sum(.input_tokens),
  median_seconds = median(.seconds),
  max_seconds = max(.seconds)
)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>    rows errors input_tokens median_seconds max_seconds
#>   <int>  <int>        <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1    10      0         1966          0.471       0.713

This small model on a CPU does not get every ticket right. The tables show speed and format, not accuracy.

A request with three questions takes a fraction of a second on this CPU. Your time depends on your computer.

Venn

Venn (venn-vdm, by Mark Russinovich, MIT license) is a research preview of a “vector decision model”: a small decision head on the open reader EmbeddingGemma 2. It answers noul, choice and score questions about a text, or about one image (experimental). It runs on a CPU, one request at a time, and needs Python 3.12. Its probabilities are not calibrated.

Start Venn

Clone https://github.com/markrussinovich/venn-vdm, then:

python -m pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
python -m pip install ".[embedding]"
venn download-embedder
venn serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

Venn and Laya use the same port. Run one of them at a time. Venn is ready when http://127.0.0.1:8000/health shows "reader":"ready".

Decisions

The task is the one of the vignette “Choosing a model”: the main injury of a report of a work injury, one of five. Here the data are all 464 reports of ohio_injuries. decider_venn() needs no key. max_active = 1 sends one request at a time, as the server answers one at a time.

nature <- question_choice(
  "Which injury does this report of a work injury describe? Choose the main injury.",
  c(
    amputation = "A body part is cut or torn off, in whole or in part.",
    fracture = "A bone is broken or cracked.",
    `crushing injury` = "A body part is squeezed hard between objects, and the tissue is damaged.",
    `thermal burn` = "Heat, flame, hot liquid or a hot surface burns the skin.",
    concussion = "A blow or a shake to the head hurts the brain."
  )
)
venn <- decider_venn()
answers <- decide(venn, nature, text = ohio_injuries$final_narrative, max_active = 1)

Venn reports no tokens and no cost, so .input_tokens and .cost are NA.

Calibration

A calibrator learns how to change the probabilities of a model so that they match the share of right answers. It must learn on rows that it does not score. So the 464 rows go into two halves (rsample::initial_split(), which stratifies by the larger classes and puts the small ones at random): probably fits the calibrator on one half, and yardstick scores the other half before and after.

classes <- names(nature@answers)
answers <- answers |>
  dplyr::mutate(truth = factor(ohio_injuries$collapsed_nature_title, levels = classes))
set.seed(2026)
halves <- rsample::initial_split(answers, prop = 0.5, strata = truth)
fit_half <- rsample::training(halves)
score_half <- rsample::testing(halves)
calibrator <- probably::cal_estimate_multinomial(
  fit_half,
  truth = truth,
  estimate = dplyr::starts_with(".pred_") & !dplyr::all_of(".pred_class"),
  smooth = FALSE
)
calibrated <- probably::cal_apply(score_half, calibrator, pred_class = .pred_class)
score <- function(x, stage) {
  probabilities <- as.matrix(dplyr::select(x, dplyr::starts_with(".pred_") & !dplyr::all_of(".pred_class")))
  tibble::tibble(
    stage = stage,
    accuracy = yardstick::accuracy_vec(x$truth, x$.pred_class),
    roc_auc = yardstick::roc_auc_vec(x$truth, probabilities),
    brier = yardstick::brier_class_vec(x$truth, probabilities),
    mean_top_probability = mean(apply(probabilities, 1, max))
  )
}
dplyr::bind_rows(
  score(score_half, "before calibration"),
  score(calibrated, "after calibration")
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   stage              accuracy roc_auc  brier mean_top_probability
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>                <dbl>
#> 1 before calibration    0.858   0.976 0.191                 0.524
#> 2 after calibration     0.953   0.989 0.0379                0.971

The calibrator has the answers of the question as its levels, so it can go into a setup: decide() then applies it to every answer.

venn_setup <- decision_setup(venn, nature, calibrator = calibrator)

Before calibration, the most likely answer of Venn has a mean probability of about one half, though most of its answers are right: its probabilities rank the answers well, but they are too low. The calibrator, fitted on the other half, makes the probabilities match the share of right answers (a much lower Brier score), and the most likely answer after calibration is right more often. Without a calibrator, Venn is right less often than the hosted models of “Choosing a model” (on 75 of these reports), and a calibrator needs labeled rows. Venn is a research preview: check it on your own data before you use it.

Privacy

decide() sends each text to the URL of the decider. With http://localhost:8000, the text goes to your own computer and to no one else. Use a local server when the texts are private.
